articles.title: The Death of the Prompt: Why Autonomous Agents Are the Real Paradigm Shift in Python Development
articles.excerpt: We’ve all been there. You spend hours meticulously engineering a prompt. You add a few "few-shot" examples, inject some XML tags to keep the output formatted, and wrap it in a clean Python script usin…
articles.body: We’ve all been there. You spend hours meticulously engineering a prompt. You add a few "few-shot" examples, inject some XML tags to keep the output formatted, and wrap it in a clean Python script using the OpenAI SDK. It works brilliantly for the exact test case you wrote. Then, you hand it to a user, they type something slightly unexpected, the model hallucinates, your regex parser crashes on unescaped JSON, and your morning is ruined. Welcome to the ceiling of prompt engineering. For the past few years, the software engineering world has treated Large Language Models (LLMs) like high-tech oracles: you ask a question, and you hope you get a pristine answer. But as developers attempt to build complex, production-ready AI applications, a glaring limitation has become impossible to ignore.

articles.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation for System Design, With Worked Examples
articles.excerpt: System design estimation is a way to turn an ambiguous product description into approximate traffic, storage, bandwidth, and capacity requirements. The goal is not to predict an exact production numbe…
articles.body: System design estimation is a way to turn an ambiguous product description into approximate traffic, storage, bandwidth, and capacity requirements. The goal is not to predict an exact production number. It is to expose the order of magnitude, make assumptions visible, and identify which part of the design deserves attention first. A useful estimate follows a repeatable sequence: define the workload, calculate average and peak requests per second, split reads from writes, estimate data growth, calculate network throughput, and translate the results into design choices. The arithmetic should be simple enough to explain aloud and detailed enough for another engineer to challenge.

articles.title: My Store Turned Into Wingdings for Exactly One Reason, and It Was 3,410 Bytes
articles.excerpt: On 7 November 2026 I added analytics to my store and rewarded myself by breaking the entire site's text. Every word on every page rendered as garbled symbols in my browser. The build was fine. The fil…
articles.body: On 7 November 2026 I added analytics to my store and rewarded myself by breaking the entire site's text. Every word on every page rendered as garbled symbols in my browser. The build was fine. The files were fine. The words were fine, somewhere underneath whatever my browser had decided they were. The site is a small store built with Astro, deployed on Vercel. The change that morning was tiny and boring: install Vercel Analytics, drop the component into the base layout, deploy. The kind of change you make between sips of tea. Then I opened the store and it looked like the text had been fed through a paper shredder and reassembled by an enemy. What I checked first (all wrong) I checked the content files. Clean. I checked the build output locally. Clean. I rebuilt.

articles.title: Uranus has a weird magnetic field that's stumped scientists for 40 years — we may finally know why
articles.excerpt: The lopsided magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune could be the product of extreme conditions inside the planets, increasing the electrical conductivity that enhances the dynamo effect.
articles.body: The posided magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may stem from extreme conditions lying within their deep interior. Unravelling the mystery behind the magnetic fields of these worlds is giving us new insight into the little-known interiors of the ice giants. Only one spacecraft has ever visited Uranus and Neptune, the Voyager 2 spacecraft which spend past Uranus in January 1986 and Neptune in August 1989. Voyager 2 found that their planetary magnetic fields were, to put it bluntly, wonky. Uranus’ magnetic field was offset from its rotational axis by 59 degrees and isn’t even centered on the planet’s core, but instead is only two-thirds of the way down.

articles.title: Were there 'lost cosmonauts' in the early Soviet space program?
articles.excerpt: At the height of the Cold War, two amateur radio operators alleged they intercepted signals from Soviet cosmonauts who perished during missions that remained secret.
articles.body: In the final weeks of 1960, two young radio enthusiasts were monitoring transmissions from a home-built listening station on a rooftop in Turin, Italy, when the brothers detected something extraordinary: a faint signal that bore the hallmarks of one originating from space. That wasn't the only surprising thing about the alleged signal:, the transmission carried a very familiar message: it was Morse code for the international distress signal SOS. As the youths listened, the signal seemed to grow weaker. This raised a troubling possibility: could it be that the signal's source was moving farther away from Earth ?

articles.title: NASA Scientists Show How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds
articles.excerpt: The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA as…
articles.body: 5 min read NASA Scientists Show How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. Now two studies led by NASA astrophysicists show in new detail how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets — worlds beyond our solar system — throughout our galaxy. Watch to learn how the presence of a planet modifies the gravitational wave signal from tightly orbiting white dwarfs. The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory could detect a Jupiter-mass planet in such systems up to thousands of light-years away.

articles.title: A robot just built a structure autonomously in space for the 1st time ever
articles.excerpt: A robot built part of an antenna in orbit recently, showcasing skills that could potentially allow the assembly of space telescopes and other large structures off Earth.
articles.body: A robot just played Tinkertoys in space, assembling the first satellite structure ever made without a human touching the controls. The DARPA-funded project saw a robotic "truss builder" create a reflective antenna using Kapton film, composite fiber tubes and aluminum joints. The implications are huge for future missions, potentially opening up new possibilities to build — or fix — satellites in the final frontier. "This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space ," Sergio Pellegrino, an aerospace and civil engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement on Nov. 5 .
